name: Warm-water bathing

card.summary: Showering or bathing in warm rather than hot water, practised to limit skin dryness and keep skin looking smoother and more comfortable.
card.note: Very hot water raises safety concerns such as drowsiness and, in hot tubs, infection risk if poorly maintained.

quick.overview:
Warm-water bathing is a skincare-adjacent habit: choosing warm instead of hot water and keeping baths short, with the aim of avoiding the dry, tight skin people associate with hot showers.

Dermatology guidance from the American Academy of Dermatology recommends warm water and short bathing times for dry skin, followed by moisturiser on damp skin. Experimental studies on warm-water bathing mostly examine circulation, sleep and relaxation rather than appearance.
quick.how: Practitioners use lukewarm-to-warm water, limit showers and baths to roughly five to ten minutes per AAD guidance, pat dry, and apply a fragrance-free moisturiser while skin is still damp.
quick.risks: Warm bathing is low risk. Very hot water can cause drowsiness, and poorly sanitised hot tubs have been linked to folliculitis and legionellosis. The US CPSC recommends water not exceed 40 C (104 F).

lead: Warm-water bathing is the habit of washing in warm rather than hot water to avoid drying the skin. People adopt it as part of a skincare routine so that skin stays more hydrated and looks smoother.

The American Academy of Dermatology advises warm water, baths and showers of about five to ten minutes, patting skin dry, and moisturising right after while skin is damp, with a fragrance-free cream or ointment.[1] Wikipedia's article on dry skin lists frequent washing with harsh soaps among the contributors and recommends patting dry and using emollients.[2]
Scientific studies of warm-water bathing mostly investigate other outcomes, such as peripheral circulation, sleep quality and exercise tolerance.[3][4]

chain: Warm instead of hot, shorter bathing
Moisturiser locks in water on damp skin
Skin that looks and feels less dry
angle.text: Keeping water warm and bathing brief is part of dermatologist-style guidance for dry skin; people use it to keep skin hydrated and smoother-looking between moisturising routines.

paras: The habit contrasts with long, hot showers. AAD guidance for dry skin recommends warm water, limiting baths and showers to five to ten minutes, closing the bathroom door to keep humidity, patting skin dry, using a gentle cleanser only where needed, and shaving at the end of the shower.[1]
Dry skin is attributed to low humidity, frequent washing with harsh soaps, detergents and some health factors. Emollients and occlusives such as petrolatum are described as effective for relief.[2]

Water well above body temperature can cause drowsiness. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission recommends hot tub water never exceed 40 C, and 37 C is described as safe for a healthy adult. Poorly sanitised hot tubs have been linked to hot tub folliculitis and Legionnaires' disease.[5]

Studies of warm-water bathing mostly measure non-cosmetic outcomes. A pilot study of ten men compared half-body, low-leg and foot bathing for effects on peripheral circulation,[3] and a randomised pilot trial examined bicarbonate baths and sleep quality.[4] No trial in the appearance literature has compared warm and hot water for skin look.
